abstract:

authors: Anh-Khoa Dinh-Duc, Duc-Tai Dinh, Tam V. Nguyen, Minh-Triet Tran
abstract:

Abstract: CLIP's visual encoder produces only global image representations, limiting its use in region-level tasks. title: Preserving Anatomical Continuity: Three-Stage Pipeline for Colon Segmentation in 3D Abdominal CT Scans
authors: Deshan Kalupahana, Sonit Singh, Praveen Ravindran, Arcot Sowmya
abstract:
arXiv:2610.03467v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Accurate colon segmentation from CT images is essential for colorectal disease analysis, yet deep learning based methods often produce disconnected predictions due to complex anatomy. This study introduces a three-stage, topology-preserving segmentation pipeline to address this issue. The first stage performs initial deep learning-based segmentation, followed by centreline bridging to reconnect disjoint regions and a reconstruction stage to refine continuity. Evaluations on TotalSegmentator and RAOS datasets using overlap, distance and topology-based metrics demonstrate improved structural consistency while maintaining segmentation accuracy. title: Cryo-Bench: Benchmarking Foundation Models for Cryosphere Mapping

Abstract: Scene coordinate regression (SCR) achieves strong performance in outdoor LiDAR localization, but it usually requires scene-specific training that can take days, limiting practical deployment. abstract:

Abstract: Distinct pre-trained models specialized for the same task converge to closely similar behavior, yet the parameter updates that produce it share no common coordinate system. abstract:

title: Nearest-neighbour baselines for fingerprint prediction from MS/MS spectra under different assumptions
authors: Ling Min Serena Khoo
abstract:
arXiv:2610.02249v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: It has recently been shown that nearest-neighbour retrieval provides a strong baseline for molecular fingerprint prediction from MS/MS spectra, with several variants matching or outperforming current deep learning models (Khoo and Barzilay, 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Gupta et al., 2026). Importantly, "nearest neighbour" encompasses a family of retrieval methods that differ in the information assumed to be available at inference. In this report, we systematically compare several nearest-neighbour variants and show how these differing assumptions affect performance. Our goal is to establish stricter baselines that enable more rigorous benchmarking and better measure progress in this area.

authors: Yair Shenfeld, Ricardo Baptista, Stefano Peluchetti
abstract:
arXiv:2610.02754v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion models are highly developed in continuous spaces for image and video domains. Recently, major advances have been made for discrete diffusion models for categorical data, specifically in the language domain. In contrast, diffusion models for discrete integer-valued data are less developed, despite the prevalence of this modality, ranging from images and music to gene counts. This is the first family of diffusion models for ordinal data which centers around training denoisers, which at the same time allows for bi-directional (up and down) perturbations of the data. The simplicity of the training objective, combined with the flexibility of bi-directional perturbations, leads us to obtain competitive results across different data modalities.

Abstract: Jazz pianists develop distinctive traits that experienced listeners can often identify within seconds, yet the features underlying this recognition resist formal description. title: FASTDIAR: Frame-level speaker encoder for Streaming Diarization
authors: Nikita Torgashov, Okan K\"op\"ukl\"u
abstract:
arXiv:2610.02941v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Real-time conversational agents require speaker diarization that streams and runs on a CPU. Most systems apply an utterance-level speaker encoder to short, heavily overlapping chunks, which wastes computation and leaves the model optimized for the wrong task. We instead turn a state-of-the-art speaker recognition architecture into a causal frame-level encoder that reads the stream once and emits one embedding every 80~ms from a bounded two-second window of past audio, and pair it with online clustering that gates every update on the self-similarity of the stream. title: MintEval: Do LLMs Implement the Trading Strategy You Asked For? A Behavioural-Equivalence Benchmark for Natural-Language-to-Strategy Code
authors: Siyu Wang, Yifan Wang, Yuecheng He
abstract:
arXiv:2610.03080v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Large language models are moving from producing trading signals to writing the code that executes them. The failure mode of the second role is silent: generated code runs, a backtest plots, yet the risk logic that the trader described is not the logic being executed. Existing code benchmarks test functional correctness on unit tests and finance benchmarks test forecasting; neither measures whether an implementation behaves like the strategy that was asked for. We introduce MintEval, a benchmark in which reference strategies are generated programmatically from a library of composable building blocks, back-translated into colloquial trader instructions, and re-implemented by the model under test. title: Invariance of Clustering Operations in Causal Effect Identification
authors: Jani Nyk\"anen, Otto Tabell, Santtu Tikka, Juha Karvanen
abstract:
arXiv:2610.03101v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Clustering variables in causal graphs reduces the size of the graph and simplifies causal inference. However, arbitrary clustering can alter crucial causal relations among variables and lead to erroneous conclusions. While the identifiability of a causal effect in the clustered graph implies the identifiability in the original graph under mild conditions, nonidentifiability in clustered graph does not imply nonidentifiability in the original graph without further assumptions. When both identifiability and nonidentifiability are preserved, the clustering operation is called identification invariant. We present a broad class of clustering operations that are identification invariant based on conditions related to the c-components of the original graph. Finally, we demonstrate use of the results in practical settings.

title: ParaGeo: Decomposing Paralinguistic Variation into a Shared Latent Geometry
authors: Yuhan Liu, Yuxuan Ou, Ruoxi Su, Mohamed Ahmed Zaki, Yunbo Long
abstract:

Abstract: Speech delivery varies with both the requested paralinguistic attribute and the linguistic content. We introduce ParaGeo, a matched-content decomposition of paralinguistic variation in a frozen speech language model. Synthesized audio tokens are replayed with a fixed listening prompt; pooled key/value (K/V) representations are centered and projected into a shared low-dimensional space. Our GLM-4-Voice probe spans 80 requested controls from 12 benchmark families across eight sentences. Abstract: Feature selection for imbalanced classification tasks such as credit card fraud and consumer default detection requires balancing predictive relevance, inter-feature redundancy, and computational feasibility. authors: Francisco Escudero Guti\'errez, Junseo Lee, Sebastian Zur
abstract:

Abstract: We establish lower bounds for Hamiltonian property testing with access to the time-evolution operator but not its inverse. Each experiment may query the time-evolution operator multiple times, and distances between Hamiltonians are measured in the normalized Frobenius norm.
  In this model, we show that testing whether a Hamiltonian is $k$-local or $\varepsilon$-far from every $k$-local Hamiltonian requires $\Omega(1/\varepsilon^2)$ total evolution time, matching the upper bound of Kallaugher and Liang (TQC'25). title: DAWIS: Data Assimilation with Windowed Inverse Sampling via Multitask Interpolants
authors: Erik Wikingsson, Martin Andrae, Tomas Landelius, Fredrik Lindsten
abstract:
arXiv:2610.03314v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Flow- and diffusion-based generative models have recently emerged as flexible and highly efficient forecasting models for dynamical systems. When combined with inference-time guidance, they offer a promising route to high-dimensional non-Gaussian data assimilation (DA), the problem of combining forecasts with observations to estimate latent system states. Existing filters, however, condition on a fixed history and assimilate only the most recent observation, leaving them unable to revise past states when new observations arrive. Estimates then stay tethered to a history that later observations may contradict, and errors accumulate over the assimilation run. title: When Is Accuracy Evidence? A Unified Theory of Generalisation, Validation, and Information Fusion
authors: JM Gorriz
abstract:
arXiv:2610.03465v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: K-fold cross-validation (CV) is widely used as evidence of out-of-sample performance, although folds are neither independent experiments nor equally informative under heterogeneous data. Cross Upper-Bound Validation (CUBV) replaces point-wise CV accuracy by conservative upper bounds on true risk. Here we generalise CUBV through a single exponential framework in which the moment-generating function of the generalisation gap is controlled by a cumulant envelope gamma(lambda). This yields a family of risk bounds covering Hoeffding-, Bernstein-, dependency-aware, PAC-Bayesian, and heterogeneous source-fusion settings. For K-fold CV, dependence between fold-wise gaps is modelled through a joint sub-Gaussian proxy matrix. title: From Benchmarks to Production: A Text-to-SQL System for Complex Financial Data
authors: Arijit Sehanobish, Bruno Gomes Coelho, Guillaume Michel, Sophia Zhi, Valerie Faucon-Morin, Kristen Howell
abstract:
arXiv:2610.03524v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: General-purpose Text-to-SQL systems achieve strong performance on academic benchmarks like Spider and BIRD, where schemas are relatively shallow and column values are often human readable. In production financial databases, where concepts are stored as opaque integer keys rather than human-readable strings, these methods fall below 50%, as even simple queries require multiple joins and filter predicates reference opaque IDs. title: EEGDM: Learning EEG Representation with Latent Diffusion Model
authors: Shaocong Wang, Tong Liu, Yihan Li, Ming Li, Kairui Wen, Pei Yang, Wenqi Ji, Minjing Yu, Yong-Jin Liu
abstract:

Abstract: Recent advances in self-supervised learning for EEG representation have largely relied on masked reconstruction, where models are trained to recover randomly masked signal segments. While effective at modeling local dependencies, the training objective of masked reconstruction does not compel the model to capture global generative constraints essential for characterizing neural activity. Abstract: We compare Ising ({-1, +1}) and QUBO ({0, 1}) encodings for Boltzmann machine learning under controlled protocols that fix the sampler, optimizer, and learning-rate design within each comparison. abstract:

Abstract: We present a theoretical study of the robustness of parameterized neural networks to random input perturbations. title: Identify then Realize: Contrastive Learning of Latent Port-Hamiltonian Dynamics from Partial Observations
authors: Peilun Li, Kaiyuan Tan, Daniel Moyer, Thomas Beckers
abstract:
arXiv:2605.16682v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Identifying latent state representations and dynamics is essential when direct modeling in observation space is infeasible, particularly under partial and high-dimensional observations. In such settings, representation learning and physics-aware modeling are inherently coupled. We propose CIPHER, a two-stage identify-then-realize framework for learning latent port-Hamiltonian models of conservative and dissipative systems. First, a contrastive teacher jointly learns an encoder and a neural ODE to obtain predictive state representations from observation histories. Second, a student learns an invertible nonlinear coordinate transformation and port-Hamiltonian dynamics by matching encoded observed futures. authors: Alfred M. Pastor, Maribel Castillo, Jose M. Badia
abstract:

Abstract: Classical simulation remains essential for developing and validating quantum algorithms, but its cost grows rapidly with circuit size. Tensor-network contraction can reduce this cost by exploiting circuit structure, although its efficiency depends strongly on the chosen contraction plan. On GPUs, plans with similar theoretical complexity may perform very differently because execution also depends on parallelism, reduction structure, memory traffic, and contraction geometry. Each plan is represented by structural features derived directly from its sequence of pairwise contractions, and gradient-boosted rankers are trained from GPU measurements using listwise and pairwise objectives. Abstract: Implicit Graph Neural Networks (IGNNs) define node representations as fixed points of graph neural operators, enabling effectively infinite-depth propagation, iteration-independent parameterization, and flexible test-time computation. Yet these benefits depend on the equilibrium being unique and reached by fixed-point iteration. This raises a central question: can IGNNs gain expressiveness through richer, edge-dependent transformations while retaining the inherent strengths of their equilibrium formulation? title: MASCIT: A Mask-Aware State Space Classifier for Naturally Irregular Time Series
authors: Yoo-Min Jung, Hyeon-Gi Kim, Jonghun Park
abstract:
arXiv:2609.34409v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Naturally irregular time series combine asynchronous observations, missing values, unequal lengths, and nonuniform sampling, while dense adapters can discard temporal structure. We propose a mask-aware state space classifier for irregular time series (MASCIT), which supplies observation masks to the encoder and excludes invalid steps from gated temporal aggregation. Across 34 irregular time series datasets, MASCIT yielded the strongest aggregate point estimate and was the only evaluated neural model with three-seed results on every dataset. MASCIT retained the lowest point rank across six overlapping irregularity indicators, while factorial ablations favored partial over full selectivity. These results support selective state space models as effective, executable backbones for naturally irregular time series classification.

title: Continuous Policy and Value Iteration for Relaxed Stochastic Control Problems and Its Convergence
authors: Qi Feng, Gu Wang
abstract:
arXiv:2506.08121v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We introduce a continuous policy-value iteration algorithm where the approximations of the value function of a stochastic control problem and the optimal control are simultaneously updated through Langevin-type dynamics. This paper focuses on the entropy-regularized relaxed control problem with infinite horizon. We establish policy improvement and demonstrate convergence to the optimal control under the monotonicity condition of the Hamiltonian. By utilizing Langevin-type stochastic differential equations for continuous updates along the policy iteration direction, our approach enables the use of distribution sampling techniques in machine learning to optimize the value function and identify the optimal control simultaneously. Numerical experiments are presented for LQ model with a non-concave reward, and a non-LQ example with a skewed-Laplace optimal control.

title: Estimating prevalence with precision and accuracy
authors: Aime Bienfait Igiraneza, Christophe Fraser, Robert Hinch
abstract:
arXiv:2507.06061v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Unlike classification, whose goal is to estimate the class of each data point, quantification (or prevalence estimation) aims to estimate the distribution of classes in a dataset. An important task in prevalence estimation is to quantify the uncertainty in prevalence estimates. In this paper, we introduce Precise Quantifier (PQ), a Bayesian aggregative quantifier that achieves narrow prediction intervals with sufficient coverage (i.e., sufficient proportion of intervals containing the true prevalence). We find that PQ produces more precise prevalence estimates than existing methods as the discriminative power of the underlying classifier increases and as the validation-to-test size ratio increases. These empirical results suggest that PQ uses validation information more effectively to quantify uncertainty in prevalence estimates than existing approaches.

title: Cocoon: A System Architecture for Differentially Private Training with Correlated Noises
authors: Donghwan Kim, Xin Gu, Jinho Baek, Timothy Lo, Younghoon Min, Kwangsik Shin, Jongryool Kim, Jongse Park, Kiwan Maeng
abstract:

Abstract: Machine learning (ML) models memorize and leak training data, causing serious privacy issues to data owners. However, these algorithms add noise at each training iteration and degrade accuracy, limiting their real-world adoption. title: Fragmentation is Efficiently Learnable by Quantum Neural Networks
authors: Mikhail Mints, Eric R. Anschuetz
abstract:
arXiv:2512.00751v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: In certain classes of physical quantum systems, the exponentially large state space "fragments" into many low-dimensional, dynamically disconnected subspaces. We introduce a learning problem known as fragment classification, where given a quantum state input, one is interested in classifying to which subspace the state belongs. We prove that solving this learning problem is efficient on a quantum computer when the fragmentation phenomenon satisfies certain conditions. Furthermore, we give evidence supporting the classical hardness of this task by demonstrating that known dequantization techniques fail for the fragment classification problem. Consequently, this work provides a rare example of a physically motivated quantum machine learning task that is both efficient for quantum computers to perform and admits no known classical dequantization.

Abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models maintain a growing attention key-value (KV) cache, making memory a key bottleneck for long video generation. Recently, clustering-based quantization has emerged as an effective method to compress video KV caches by grouping similar key and value vectors then quantizing residual errors. Abstract: We present Neural Voxel Dynamics, a self-supervised framework for learning 3D latent dynamics from monocular video. Abstract: Diagnostic classifiers and imaging biomarkers are fitted on the embeddings of medical foundation models. These models are replaced as new versions appear. authors: Harsha Patnala, Debopriyo Banerjee, Ayush Sunil Munot, Somak Aditya
abstract:

Abstract: Structured visual reasoning, such as image puzzles, demands fine-grained visual perception, which current Vision Language Models (VLMs) often lack. authors: Rafael M. Mamede, Pedro C. Neto, Ana F. Sequeira
abstract:

Abstract: Deepfake detectors remain vulnerable to transfer-based black-box attacks, in which adversarial examples are generated on a source surrogate model and transferred to a target model, unknown to the attacker. authors: Souptik Sen, Zahra Ahmadi
abstract:

Abstract: Audio-visual models improve egocentric action recognition by exploiting complementary cues, yet typically assume that both streams remain available at inference. Existing missing-modality methods operate on trimmed, single-event clips in which a stream is entirely present or absent, whereas real sensors fail and recover within long, untrimmed observations. title: DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics
authors: Manthan Patel, Jonas Frey, Mayank Mittal, Fan Yang, Alexander Hansson, Amir Bar, Cesar Cadena, Marco Hutter
abstract:

Abstract: Depth sensors are widely deployed across robotic platforms, and advances in fast, high-fidelity depth simulation have enabled robotic policies trained on depth observations to achieve robust sim-to-real transfer for a wide range of tasks. title: Playing the network backward: A Game Theoretic Attribution Framework
authors: Jakob Paul Zimmermann, Jim Berend, Georg Loho, Sebastian Lapuschkin, Wojciech Samek
abstract:
arXiv:2605.06212v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Attribution methods explain which input features drive a model's prediction, making them central to model debugging and mechanistic interpretability. authors: Devroop Kar, Daniel Krutz, Travis Desell
abstract:

Abstract: Hybrid quantum classical neural networks integrate parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs) with established deep learning architectures, but their performance depends strongly on the choice of quantum circuit architecture, a choice that remains largely manual. Abstract: Robots need to anticipate how their actions will change the world, since manipulation success hinges on the resulting contacts and object motions. Abstract: Modern machine learning models are typically trained on data assumed to be representative of the predictive tasks the model will face in the future, but practical datasets violate this assumption. Abstract: Forecasting rare, high-cost events in multivariate time-series systems is hard because their precursors are seldom observed, so a purely data-driven model has little to learn from. authors: Marcel Binz, Eric Schulz

title: Shared Canonical Component Removal Beyond Expert Views
authors: Jose Roberto Tello Ayala, Akl C. Fahed, Roy Perlis, Finale Doshi-Velez
abstract:

Abstract: In clinical practice, experts often begin by converting raw inputs into a set of expert features before making a decision. authors: Zeru Zhu, Marco Gamarra, Ji Liu
abstract:
arXiv:2610.12697v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: This paper studies an open network design problem of constructing graph topologies with maximum algebraic connectivity under fixed numbers of vertices and edges. A density-dependent approach is proposed that decomposes the design task into two stages: a high-quality, low-cost structural backbone construction and a reinforcement learning completion stage. The method selects the backbone based on density, using complete multipartite graphs in dense regimes and Cayley graphs in low-to-intermediate regimes, and then refines the remaining edges through a learning-based procedure. Numerical results show that the proposed method achieves high algebraic connectivity with favorable runtime scalability, outperforming existing methods. These results support a structural-family-first strategy for scalable network design.

title: Product Monte Carlo: Expectation Under a Product of Densities
authors: Pietro Carlotti, Sifan Liu, Yuling Yao
abstract:

Abstract: Aggregating independently computed sub-sample inferences is a well-known challenge in large-scale Bayesian computation, federated learning, and opinion pooling. The core problem is to approximate a distribution whose density is proportional to a product of individual densities. We propose Product Monte Carlo (PMC), an algorithm for computing arbitrary expectations under a product of densities using only Monte Carlo draws from individual densities. We turn the intractable product expectation into a regression problem by expressing it through a family of computable conditional expectations. Besides the point estimate, our fully Bayesian regression formulation provides coherent uncertainty quantification and principled diagnostics. We establish theoretical guarantees on consistency and characterize convergence rates for the PMC estimator. title: PVBRF-ID: Private, Verifiable and Byzantine-Robust Federated Intrusion Detection for Oilfield Enterprise Networks
authors: Mustafa S. Aljumaily, Ali Ataeemh Allami, Mustafa N. Mnati, Nawar S. Alseelawi, Shahab Abdulla
abstract:

Abstract: Federated learning allows dispersed oilfield sites to train a shared intrusion detector without pooling network traffic, yet its aggregation step forces a choice between privacy and robustness. Byzantine-robust rules must read each update in the clear, whereas secure aggregation hides updates from the checks that detect poisoning. We present PVBRF-ID, a two-server protocol in which sites secret-share their updates and the servers jointly test each update's norm and its cosine similarity to a reference computed on a small clean root set, revealing one accept bit per site. Commitments, Merkle roots and a homomorphic audit make the inclusion of accepted updates publicly verifiable. On a 15-class Edge-IIoTset task with ten sites holding differently distributed data and ten random seeds, PVBRF-ID matched FedAvg on clean data (macro-F1 0.708 vs. 0.706) and withstood sign-flip attacks (0.696 vs. 0.091). title: A Distributional Framework for Behavioral Characterization and Risk Management of Large Language Models
authors: David Garc\'ia-Lorite, Raul Merino
abstract:
arXiv:2610.12718v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Large language models are stochastic by nature. Repeated executions under the same experimental conditions may produce different responses. We propose a framework that can be applied across the model lifecycle, from task design to residual behavior and continuous monitoring. The method consists of building an empirical response distribution estimated through Monte Carlo simulation. Semantic interventions are introduced to study how these distributions change. We illustrate the framework with two different tasks, borrower classification and music album recommendation, and quantify the resulting distributional changes. The framework is linked to model risk management and governance by measuring robustness and control effectiveness, and characterizing residual behavior. Since it relies only on observed responses, it can also be applied to black-box models accessed through commercial APIs.

title: Scalable Learning of Determinantal Point Processes with Kernel-Structured Interactions
authors: Takahiro Kawashima, Hideitsu Hino
abstract:
arXiv:2610.12829v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Determinantal point processes (DPPs) on a finite set are probability models that exhibit repulsion where inter-item similarities are encoded by a positive definite kernel matrix. Scaling DPP learning to large datasets typically requires imposing structural constraints on the kernel matrix, such as a low-rank-plus-diagonal form. However, structural assumptions introduce a severe trade-off between expressive power and computational scalability. Our study addresses this challenge by (a) modeling the full-rank interactions via a nonlinear kernel function and latent features, (b) designing a surrogate function for the maximum likelihood estimator, and (c) adopting stochastic optimization using random features of the nonlinear kernel. Numerical experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that our method significantly improves this trade-off, achieving better generalization performance with remarkable parameter efficiency.

title: Scaling Empowered Agents
authors: Catherine Ji, Vivek Myers, Joshua Lin, Alexandra Wingate, Sergey Levine, Benjamin Eysenbach
abstract:
arXiv:2610.13002v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Empowerment measures the capacity of an agent to actively control its environment. In this work, we explain the connection between skill learning and empowerment. While skill learning is not empowerment, we introduce a simple scalable recipe for empowerment maximization: empowerment corresponds to the number of executable skills from a state, so maximizing empowerment corresponds to reaching states that are good starting points for many skills. Our recipe applies to arbitrary underlying skill learning methods. Whereas most prior work on empowerment looks at tabular settings, this recipe enables us to study empowerment at a scale where we can realize theoretically-predicted but empirically-elusive properties of empowerment (e.g., gathering resources, environment modification, survival). authors: Po-Heng Chou, Jen-Yu Chiu, Chun-Yu Yeh, Wei-Lung Mao, Walid Saad
abstract:

Abstract: Consumer rotating devices, including washing machines, air conditioners, electric fans, robotic vacuum cleaners, and home fitness equipment, increasingly rely on vibration sensing for intelligent condition monitoring and predictive maintenance. Ensuring reliable operation in these resource-constrained appliances requires efficient, lightweight artificial intelligence (AI) solutions capable of processing non-stationary signals under real-world operational interference. This paper proposes a lightweight AI-assisted vibration sensing framework that employs continuous wavelet transform (CWT) and Hilbert-Huang transform (HHT) to convert one-dimensional (1-D) vibration time-series signals into two-dimensional (2-D) time-frequency representations. title: CoBe: A Benchmark For Conversational Counterfactual Text Editing
authors: Arvind Raghavan, Inwoo Hwang, Shreyas Havaldar, Kai-Zhan Lee, Aurghya Maiti, Yushu Pan, Jeffrey Wu, Mingxuan Li, Elias Bareinboim
abstract:

Abstract: Counterfactual text editing is the ability to revise a given text in light of a hypothetical change while preserving facts not causally affected by that change. When asked what would have happened if a doctor had not recommended surgery, the model output should retain the patient's medical history and modify only the consequences of the decision. This requires causal understanding: a model must determine, without being explicitly instructed to, what events are affected by the hypothetical change and what should remain fixed. This skill is central to human reasoning, especially in safety-critical domains like healthcare or law. By contrast, the task of associational text generation merely generates text statistically associated with the altered condition. authors: Snigdha Chandan Khilar
abstract:

Abstract: Model providers now face distillation campaigns run through thousands of accounts, each of which looks like an ordinary user. When network and payment metadata cannot link those accounts, the only evidence left is what they ask. We study what a provider can and cannot learn from those queries alone, using one million real chat turns for development and 17 later weeks that no design choice touched for a single frozen evaluation. The answer is set less by anything specific to extraction than by benign coordination: a campaign is visible only if it is more distinctive than the most distinctive group of ordinary users in the same week. We make this precise, show that a small but positive difference between campaign and users buys a detection time rather than detectability, and identify the campaign that is hardest to detect. authors: Mohammad Khalooei, Mohammad Sabokrou
abstract:
arXiv:2610.13112v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) frequently exhibit object hallucination, affirming absent sounds. The dominant mitigation, Audio-Aware Decoding (AAD), contrasts logits under real audio against an all-zero "blank" waveform, flagged by prior review as out-of-distribution. title: Fast Gradient-Based Approximation of Continuous Dynamic Time Warping
authors: Pierre Houedry, Romain Tavenard, Nicolas Courty, Romaric Gaudel
abstract:
arXiv:2610.13129v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) is a common choice for measuring the discrepancy between time series. It proceeds by finding an optimal warping between timestamps through dynamic programming, which can be slow and is not differentiable. Consequently, several variants have been proposed. Among them, Soft-DTW proposes a smooth formulation of DTW, amenable to gradient computation, while Continuous-DTW (CDTW) introduces a continuous formulation through parametrizable warping functions. Yet, computational costs remain high for both methods and impractical for large datasets in modern machine learning pipelines. This paper revisits CDTW in several ways. authors: Ionut Adrian Rotaru

Abstract: We present Neurograf v1, an experimental end-to-end Romanian-first language-model pipeline developed to investigate the feasibility of training language models from scratch for a lower-resource European language. authors: Mohammad Siavashi, Pascal Schwinte, Ali Banaei, Gerald Q. Maguire Jr., Marco Chiesa, Dejan Kosti\'c
abstract:
arXiv:2610.13325v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Agentic workloads resend long contexts that barely change between calls. Prefix caching now skips most of their prefill, yet every request must still be tokenized in full before the cache can even be consulted. Tokenization, a CPU stage long treated as negligible, becomes the largest part of time-to-first-token (TTFT), and a frontend that tokenizes for a whole GPU fleet limits how many GPUs it can feed. We present GraphTok, a GPU tokenizer that runs the entire encoding pipeline, from pre-tokenization through byte-pair encoding (BPE) merging to token-ID assembly, as one replayable CUDA graph. GraphTok reproduces the reference token IDs bit-for-bit on GPT-2, Llama 3, Qwen 2.5, DeepSeek-V3, and Gemma 3, hands short inputs to a CPU engine where the GPU cannot win, and plugs into unmodified vLLM and NVIDIA Dynamo. authors: Xu He, Homayoon Beigi
abstract:

Abstract: Recent accent classification systems can achieve high accuracy in standard in-corpus evaluations. However, when speakers overlap between the training and test sets, such results may overestimate model robustness compared with real-world deployment scenarios. This study revisits the robustness of DistilHuBERT-based accent classification by using L2-ARCTIC and multiple external English accent datasets. abstract:

Abstract: In machine learning, a self-attention dynamics describes the attention mechanism of transformers, and is obtained treating the layer index of a transformer as time index. Scope of this paper is to provide a thorough investigation of the discrete-time version of the self-attention dynamics: a complete classification of its equilibria is given, and their stability properties are studied, in both the single-head and the multihead case. title: Scalable Sparse Autoregressive Variational Inference for Non-Gaussian Spatial Fields
authors: Paul F. V. Wiemann, Matthias Katzfuss
abstract:
arXiv:2610.13656v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Latent field models are essential for spatial statistics, but the posterior distribution of the latent field, even with a Gaussian process (GP) prior, is analytically intractable whenever the likelihood is non-Gaussian. Existing approximations are either too slow or too restrictive for large non-Gaussian datasets. We present a scalable variational inference framework that mirrors the sparse nearest-neighbor autoregressive structure of the prior in the variational family, uses normalizing-flow conditionals for expressiveness, and amortizes all variational parameters via a single shared neural conditioner. Doubly stochastic optimization with reduced ancestor sets achieves polylogarithmic complexity per iteration.

title: On the Approximation Complexity of Matrix Product Operator (MPO) Born Machines
authors: Chao Li, Zerui Tao, Yuchen Cong, Jian Xu, Qibin Zhao
abstract:
arXiv:2605.11471v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Matrix product operator Born machines (MPO-BMs) are tractable tensor-network models for probabilistic modeling, yet their approximation capabilities remain poorly understood in theory. In this paper, we characterize these capabilities from both negative and positive perspectives. As a negative result, we prove that constructing a polynomial-bond MPO-BM approximation to an arbitrary continuous target with bounded KL error is NP-hard. On the positive side, for score-based variational inference, we prove that targets satisfying a log-Sobolev inequality admit polynomial-bond MPO-BM approximations with provable KL guarantees when the loss-induced Hamiltonian is local and has a constant spectral gap. Furthermore, under the same conditions, we construct local importance-sampling estimators and prove that polynomially many local score queries suffice to preserve the KL guarantees.
